title: Hot Springs’ water
lead: The City of Hot Springs owns its water and sewer utility, paid for by water and sewer bills. It serves the city and much of unincorporated Garland County. Other parts of the county have their own systems.

facts.v: Lake Hamilton and Lake Ricks, treated at the Ouachita and Lakeside plants (public water system AR0000209).

A 15-million-gallon-a-day plant opened in April 2026 — the city’s first new water plant in close to 60 years — as part of the $155 million Lake Ouachita Water Supply Project. Voters approved the bonds ($110 million and $45 million, the latest in 2022), which added $4 to the base water rate.

Leak-finding meters and pipe listening devices helped cut water the city couldn’t account for from 44% to 24% (the meter company’s case study). S&P put it at about 20% in 2021, “down from 40% historically.”
Two treatment plants and about 713 miles of sewer lines serve more than 37,000 customers. The main plant (permit AR0033880) discharges to Lake Catherine.

facts.v: S&P noted in 2021 that the water system’s new debt more than doubled its yearly debt payments by 2023, with rate increases approved to cover it.
The North Garland County Regional Water District serves part of the county separately; Hot Springs Village has its own water system.

facts.v: The thermal water is public: the city keeps a jug fountain on Central Avenue that anyone can fill up at, free, any time of day.

quality.lead: The 2025 report lists no health-limit violations on the running averages the law uses.

rows.note: Single readings ranged up to 104 ppb — the report says the upper end went over the limit.

quality.violation: At 74 of 80, Hot Springs runs close to the chlorine-byproduct limit — the one number here worth watching.
quality.inspection: Sewer: after heavy rains in May 2025, five sewer overflows hit the Hot Springs Creek Pump Station area — one about 67,500 gallons into Hot Springs Creek — and health advisories were posted May 7–13. The city reported to the state’s enforcement office that new pumps had arrived and would be installed within months.

fits.name: Keep finding the lost water
fits.why: Hot Springs is the proof case for leak-finding meters — the same tools the guide below grades A. The next number to publish is today’s loss rate (Docket #10).

fits.name: Cut chlorine byproducts
fits.why: At 74 of 80, biological filtration and UV disinfection — both proven — would give more room under the limit.

fits.name: Stop the overflows
fits.why: Rainwater getting into old sewer lines is what overwhelms pump stations. Sealing the lines and upgrading pumps is the proven fix; the lakes pay when it isn’t done.

fits.name: Protect the lakes
fits.why: Lake Hamilton, Lake Ricks, and now Lake Ouachita supply the water, and Lake Catherine receives the treated sewage — the same lakes people swim and fish in.

question: What will the full sewer fix cost, and how is it being paid for? The records we have don’t total it yet (Docket #11).
